title: Throwing and altering a square form
subtitle: Throwing a cylinder and altering it into a square vase or planter by pressing into four sides
excerpt: Throwing and altering combines wheel-throwing speed with hand-building form flexibility. A cylinder is thrown on the wheel and then altered off the wheel into a non-circular shape by pressing, paddling, or faceting the walls. This pattern produces a square vase form in stoneware: a technically demanding piece that requires both throwing accuracy and confident alteration.
sourceNotes: Throw-and-alter technique is established in studio ceramics practice from the mid-twentieth century onward. Form proportions and alteration methodology derived from studio ceramics technical reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: Working thrown clay until it runs true with no wobble at any speed: the prerequisite for consistent walls.
The technique of deforming a thrown form off the wheel: pressing, paddling, or faceting the walls into a non-circular shape.
The correct drying stage for alteration: firm enough to hold the new shape but soft enough to deform without cracking.
Cutting or pressing flat planes into a thrown form to produce angular or geometric sides.

content.text: This pattern requires a pottery wheel and kiln firing to cone 6 (approximately 1220 °C). Alteration is done off the wheel on a table or banding wheel: the piece must be at leather-hard before altering, not freshly thrown. Alteration of a still-wet form collapses the walls. Do not rush the drying time between throwing and alteration.
The square form is
altered

from a straight-sided cylinder thrown tall and narrow. The alteration phase presses four flat sides into the cylinder walls using a wooden rib or a flat paddle, working opposite sides first to maintain symmetry. The corners retain some roundness naturally: this is a feature of the thrown-and-altered process and distinguishes it from a purely slab-built square form.
Throwing the cylinder
Weigh out 900 g of smooth or grogged stoneware. Wedge 50 turns.
Centre
on a wheel bat. Open to 8 cm interior diameter: the cylinder must be narrow enough for the walls to remain parallel throughout.

Pull the walls upward in four to five passes. The target is a straight-sided cylinder, 18 to 20 cm tall, with walls 6 to 7 mm thick. Taller is better for this form: the alteration will reduce height slightly as the walls expand outward. Keep wall thickness even throughout: check with a needle tool at three points on the wall.
Compress the rim flat with a chamois. The rim must be thick enough (at least 5 mm) to survive alteration without splitting. Cut from the bat with a wire cutter.
Altering the form
Allow the cylinder to reach
leather-hard

: firm and cool to the touch, but still flexible. This takes 4 to 8 hours depending on conditions. The piece must hold the new shape when pressed and not spring back. If it springs back to round, it is too wet; wait longer.

Hold the cylinder in both hands. Identify four equally spaced points around the circumference: mark these lightly with a pin at the top rim if needed. Press the flat face of a wooden rib firmly against the first opposite pair of walls (north and south), squeezing toward the centre. The walls flatten and the cylinder takes on an oval cross-section.

Rotate 90° and press the second pair of walls (east and west) with the rib. The form now has four sides with rounded corners. The rim opens from oval toward square: it will not be fully square at this point.
Work the
facets

from base to rim in sections. At the base, press firmly; at the rim, lighter pressure only: the rim is the most vulnerable to cracking. Support the inside of the wall with the fingers of the opposite hand while pressing from outside with the rib.

Step back and view from above: the rim should be roughly square with rounded corners. Minor imbalances can be corrected by pressing lightly on the relevant side. Check that all four walls are plumb: not leaning inward or outward: by sighting from the side.
Leave the piece to stiffen to bone-dry before trimming a foot ring. Trim a square or softened-corner foot ring to match the form.

rows.cause: Clay too dry when alteration started: past leather-hard
rows.fix: Mist the exterior lightly with water and cover for 15 minutes to rehydrate. Attempt the alteration again. Cracks that open during alteration do not self-heal: reduce ambition on this piece and start a new one.

rows.cause: Clay too wet: not yet at leather-hard
rows.fix: Stop pressing immediately. Set the piece back on the bat and allow more drying time before retrying.

rows.problem: Corners sharper on one pair than the other
rows.cause: More pressure applied on the first pair of sides than the second
rows.fix: Return to the gentler pair and re-press. Always work both pairs in sequence repeatedly in small increments rather than fully pressing one pair before the other.
